rationales: The first shell can hold at most 2 electrons, not 8.
The third shell can hold at most 2n² = 2(3)² = 18 electrons.
Ten is less than the maximum capacity of the third shell.
Thirty-two is the maximum capacity of the fourth shell, not the third.
Discharge tube experiments revealed charged particles, rather than the complete structure of the atom.
Neutrons were discovered through later experiments, not discharge tube experiments.
Discharge tube experiments led to the discovery of electrons and positively charged particles identified as protons.
The presence of the nucleus was established by Rutherford’s scattering experiments.
The periodic table could accommodate isotopes; their number is not the reason they share a place.
Some isotopes are unstable, but instability does not explain why isotopes are not assigned separate places.
Isotopes have the same atomic number and therefore occupy the same position in the periodic table.
Isotopes generally show similar periodic behavior because they have the same atomic number.
Isotopes of an element have the same number of electrons in neutral atoms.
Isotopes differ in their number of neutrons.
Isotopes have the same number of protons by definition.
Electrons do not differ between neutral isotopes, so this choice is incorrect.
Oxygen-17 has 8 protons, 8 electrons, and 9 neutrons.
Oxygen-16 has 8 protons, 8 electrons, and 8 neutrons.
Oxygen-18 has 8 protons, 8 electrons, and 10 neutrons.
Oxygen-16 has equal numbers of protons, electrons, and neutrons, so this is not correct.
14.0210 is too high for the weighted average of isotopes with mass numbers 14 and 15 at the stated abundances.
This is the likely intended choice and is closest to the weighted average, though the stated abundances give approximately 14.0035, so the options appear inconsistent.
14.2100 is far above the weighted average implied by the abundances.
14.1200 is also too high for the weighted average implied by the abundances.
Radiocarbon dating estimates the age of once-living organic material from its carbon-14 content.
Radiocarbon dating estimates age, not the material’s overall composition.
Radiocarbon dating does not determine whether a material is useful.
Radiocarbon dating uses radioactive decay, but its purpose is to estimate age rather than merely identify radioactivity.
The strong nuclear force binds particles in the nucleus together.
The weak nuclear force is involved in certain particle transformations, not in holding the nucleus together.
Electrostatic repulsion acts between protons and does not bind the nucleus.
Dipolar force is not the force that holds nuclear particles together.
Electrons are not stationary around the nucleus in the model described by this question.
In the textbook’s orbital model, electrons remain around the nucleus while revolving around it.
Electron wave-like behavior is important in quantum mechanics, but it is not the explanation intended by this option set.
A magnetic field around the nucleus is not what keeps electrons away from it.
If the light isotope is 72.2% abundant, the heavier isotope is 27.8%, not 15%.
The two isotope abundances must total 100%, so the heavier isotope has abundance 100% − 72.2% = 27.8%.
Thirty-seven percent would make the total abundance 109.2%.
Seventy-two percent is approximately the abundance of the light isotope, not the heavier one.
